title: How the ampersand got its name
hook: Children once recited & as the last letter of the alphabet, and slurred its name.
peek: In 19th-century schoolrooms, the alphabet did not stop at Z. Children went on to the & sign, chanting and per se and. Said fast enough, often enough, the phrase blurred into one word: ampersand.
lede: For a long time & was taught as part of the alphabet, the last item after Z. When children recited their letters, any symbol that also formed a word by itself, such as A or I, was introduced with the Latin per se, meaning by itself. So the alphabet ended: X, Y, Z, and per se and. Run together, that became ampersand.

bullets.text: The symbol itself is far older than its name. It began as a joined-up way of writing et, Latin for and, and early forms appear in Roman writing from the first century AD.
In many italic typefaces the old shape is easy to spot: the & looks like a looping E followed by a t. Designers often enjoy giving it extra flourishes.
Dictionaries trace the word ampersand in print to the 1790s, though children were surely saying it earlier. The name is a classic case of a phrase worn down into one word by repetition.
A popular tale says the sign is named after the French physicist André-Marie Ampère, who supposedly used it in his work. There is no evidence for this, and the schoolroom origin is well documented.
